sources.title: Guidelines for the management of intra-abdominal infections

indications: Peritonitis, perforation or an acute abdomen requiring source control.
Bowel obstruction with strangulation, ischaemia or failure of conservative management.
Diagnostic uncertainty in a deteriorating patient where imaging cannot answer the question in time.
contraindications: There is rarely an absolute contraindication in a patient who needs source control. The real decision is whether operating serves this patient at all.
A frank discussion about ceiling of care and the likely outcome belongs before the incision, not after.
A stable patient whose collection can be drained percutaneously does not need a laparotomy.
preparation: Resuscitate deliberately, but do not delay source control for a physiology that will only improve once the source is controlled.
Risk-score and document it; it drives consultant presence, critical-care booking and the conversation with the family.
Cross-match, correct coagulopathy, warm the patient, catheterise, and place a nasogastric tube.
Antibiotics, and involve critical care before the operation rather than at the end of it.
positioning: Supine, arms out, with access for the anaesthetist to both arms and the neck.
Lloyd-Davies position if the pelvis or rectum may be involved, or if a stoma or on-table colonoscopy is possible.
Warming mattress and forced-air warming from the start.
equipment: Major general set, self-retaining retractor system, large packs.
Linear staplers, bowel clamps, energy device, suction with a large-bore sucker.
Stoma appliances, and temporary abdominal closure material if damage control is possible.
Cell salvage where trauma or major haemorrhage is expected.
anatomy: The abdomen is explored as compartments: supracolic, infracolic, both paracolic gutters, the lesser sac and the pelvis.
The retroperitoneum is divided into zones; in trauma, central zone I haematomas are explored, and lateral zone II and pelvic zone III haematomas are usually not, unless expanding or pulsatile.
Mobilising the duodenum (Kocher) and the left colon exposes structures the anterior approach cannot reach.
The lesser sac is entered through the gastrocolic omentum to see the pancreas and the posterior stomach.
criticalSafety: Complete the systematic exploration even after the pathology is found. Second pathologies are missed by stopping early.
Decide damage control EARLY, on physiology, not after four hours of definitive surgery in a cooling, acidotic, coagulopathic patient.
Do not close an abdomen that will develop compartment syndrome. An open abdomen managed well is better than a closed one that cannot ventilate.
structuresAtRisk: Ureters, particularly in a re-operative or inflamed pelvis
Duodenum, during mobilisation of the right colon
Bowel, during adhesiolysis - an unrecognised enterotomy is a leak
commonErrors: An incision too short for the operation being attempted.
Stopping the exploration at the first abnormality.
Persisting with definitive reconstruction in a patient who is physiologically exhausted.
Anastomosing bowel in a contaminated, hypotensive, vasopressor-dependent patient rather than forming a stoma.
complications: Prolonged ileus, malnutrition and enterocutaneous fistula.
The complications of the physiological insult: acute kidney injury, delirium, respiratory failure, venous thromboembolism.
postop: Critical care for most emergency laparotomies. The decision not to admit should be the exception that is justified.
Early enteral nutrition, thromboprophylaxis, multimodal analgesia, and a documented plan for what would trigger a return to theatre.
Daily consultant review, and re-image early if the patient is not improving as expected.
Explicit handover of what was found, what was NOT done, and what specifically worries the operating surgeon.

steps.emphasis: Include the possibility of a stoma, an open abdomen, and critical care. If the patient cannot consent, document the discussion with the family.
Prepare from nipples to mid-thigh: the incision may need to go anywhere, and a stoma may need siting.
The same discipline applies to an open survey as to a laparoscopic one: look everywhere before deciding anything.
Packs left deliberately for damage control are counted and RECORDED as retained, with the number written in the note and on the dressing.

step.lapa.damage-control.title: The damage-control decision
step.lapa.damage-control.why: The lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy is self-reinforcing. The decision to abbreviate the operation must be made while the patient still has reserve, not once they have none.
how: Decide on physiology, not on anatomy: temperature, pH, base deficit, lactate, transfusion requirement and how the anaesthetist says it is going.
Control haemorrhage by packing and direct control; control contamination by stapling off or exteriorising, without reconstruction.
Leave bowel in discontinuity. Do not anastomose.
Temporary abdominal closure, then intensive care to rewarm, correct and resuscitate. Plan a specific return time.
State the plan out loud to the anaesthetist and the theatre team, and write it in the note.
structuresAtRisk: Bowel left in discontinuity, which must be recorded so nobody is surprised at the re-look
pitfalls: Deciding on damage control after four hours instead of after forty minutes.
A temporary closure that is too tight, which produces exactly the compartment syndrome it was meant to prevent.
